step: Employer obtains AEWV accreditation from Immigration New Zealand
deadline_label: Must be approved before Job Check can be filed
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers must be accredited before they can hire a migrant on an AEWV.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Accreditation and the subsequent Job Check together take 4–8 weeks. Employers who assume a job offer alone entitles the migrant to apply face significant pipeline delays and may breach obligations to the candidate.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply for accreditation at least 3 months before the intended employee start date. Do not make a conditional offer to an overseas candidate until accreditation is in hand.
source: Immigration New Zealand – AEWV employer accreditation

step: Employer files Job Check for the specific role offered to the migrant
deadline_label: Must be approved before the migrant's AEWV application window opens
non_obvious_official_guidance: Accredited employers must submit a separate Job Check for each role to be filled by an AEWV holder.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The Job Check verifies the role meets the median wage threshold (NZ $29.66/hr as at 2024) and that genuine local recruitment was attempted. Roles below the median wage face additional requirements or may not qualify; no exceptions are made retroactively.
non_obvious_action_required: Confirm the offered salary meets the median wage before submitting. Document all local recruitment steps, as these are assessed during the Job Check. Approval typically takes 2–4 weeks.
source: Immigration New Zealand – AEWV Job Check

step: Migrant applies for Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV)
deadline_label: Apply after Job Check token is issued; allow 4+ weeks processing before intended start date
source: Immigration New Zealand – Accredited Employer Work Visa

step: Apply for partner and dependent child visas where applicable
form_name: Partner of a Worker Work Visa / Dependent Child visa (INZ online portal)
deadline_label: Apply simultaneously with or after AEWV grant; all dependants must hold a valid visa before travel
non_obvious_official_guidance: Partners and dependent children of AEWV holders may be eligible for separate visas granting stay and, in some cases, work rights in New Zealand.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Partner open work rights under the AEWV regime depend on the principal holder's wage level. Partners of migrants earning above the median wage threshold are generally eligible for an open work visa; partners below that threshold may only qualify for a visitor visa and cannot work. This wage-tier rule catches many applicants by surprise during family reunification planning.
non_obvious_action_required: Check the applicable wage tier before assuming a partner will receive work rights. Apply for all dependant visas before departing. Do not assume entry on a visitor visa if the partner intends to work.
source: Immigration New Zealand – Partner of a Worker Work Visa

step: Assess eligibility for 4-year transitional resident foreign income exemption before arrival
deadline_label: Assess before first NZ payday; exemption window starts automatically from the date of becoming a NZ tax resident
non_obvious_official_guidance: New tax residents who have not been NZ tax resident in the preceding 10 years may qualify for a 4-year exemption on most foreign-sourced income.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most new migrant workers qualify but never claim the exemption because neither the employer nor HR flags it. The 4-year window starts automatically the moment tax residency is established and cannot be paused or restarted. Overseas dividends, rental income, and interest that would otherwise be taxable in NZ are fully sheltered — but only if the exemption is identified and correctly applied from day one.
non_obvious_action_required: Obtain a NZ tax advice letter before your first NZ payday. Confirm you have not been NZ tax resident in the preceding 10 years. Ensure foreign income is not mistakenly included in early PAYE tax code declarations or returns.
source: Inland Revenue – Tax for new residents

step: Prepare documents required for IRD number application on arrival
deadline_label: Prepare before departure; apply within first 7 days of arrival to avoid no-notification PAYE rate
non_obvious_official_guidance: To apply for an IRD number, applicants must provide identity documents plus either a NZ bank account number or a NZ address.
non_obvious_actual_reality: This creates a practical chicken-and-egg problem: many banks require an IRD number to open an account, yet IRD requires a NZ bank account or address to issue the number. In practice the cycle is broken by securing documented temporary accommodation first and submitting form IR595 using that address before a bank account is open.
non_obvious_action_required: Arrange temporary accommodation with a written address confirmation before arrival. Bring a certified passport copy and the visa grant notice. Do not expect to open a NZ bank account on day one without any pre-existing NZ documentation.
source: Inland Revenue – Get an IRD number for an individual

step: Apply for IRD number from Inland Revenue
deadline_label: Apply within first 7 days of arrival; required before first payday to avoid 45% no-notification deduction rate
source: Inland Revenue – Get an IRD number for an individual

step: Complete tax code declaration (IR330) and provide IRD number to employer before first payday
deadline_label: Must be in employer's hands before the first payday
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees must complete a Tax Code Declaration (IR330) for their employer at or before the commencement of employment.
non_obvious_actual_reality: If the IR330 is not received before the first payday, the employer is legally required to deduct PAYE at the 'no-notification' rate of 45% — the top marginal rate — regardless of the employee's actual income bracket. Over-deductions are recoverable via an end-of-year assessment but cause an immediate first-month cash shortfall that is common and avoidable.
non_obvious_action_required: Complete the IR330 on or before day one of employment. For most primary employees the 'M' tax code applies. Do not wait until after receiving the first payslip to action this form.
source: Inland Revenue – Tax code declaration IR330

step: Confirm eligibility for publicly funded healthcare based on visa length
authority: Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora
deadline_label: Confirm before first GP visit to avoid being billed at the unsubsidised rate
non_obvious_official_guidance: Work visa holders with a visa valid for 2 years or more are generally eligible for publicly funded health services in New Zealand.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many migrant workers assume they need comprehensive private health insurance for all medical care. In practice, AEWV holders with a 2-year or longer visa are eligible for publicly funded hospital care and subsidised GP visits under PHO enrolment. GP visits are not free — a co-payment of approximately NZ$15–50 per visit is typical — but substantially cheaper than the unsubsidised rate charged to ineligible patients.
non_obvious_action_required: Check that the AEWV (and any dependant visas) have at least 2 years of validity remaining. Present visa documentation when registering with a GP practice to access the subsidised rate. Dependants holding their own 2-year+ visas are independently eligible.
source: Health New Zealand – Eligibility for publicly funded health services

step: Enrol with a PHO-registered GP practice to access subsidised primary care
authority: Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora / Primary Health Organisation (PHO)
source: Health New Zealand – Primary health care

step: Understand ACC coverage and automatic earner levy deduction via PAYE
deadline_label: Automatic from first day of employment; no separate registration required
non_obvious_official_guidance: All workers in New Zealand are automatically covered by the ACC no-fault accident compensation scheme from their first day of work.
non_obvious_actual_reality: New Zealand's ACC scheme eliminates the right to sue for personal injury damages in civil courts — including for serious workplace accidents. This surprises migrants from the UK, US, and Australia who expect to retain tort-claim rights. The earner levy (approximately NZ$1.60 per $100 of earnings for 2024/25) is deducted automatically via PAYE and requires no separate registration.
non_obvious_action_required: Do not purchase personal injury liability insurance expecting to file tort claims for accident injuries — this right does not exist in NZ. Understand the scope of ACC cover; mental injury arising from a physical accident is typically covered, but pure psychiatric harm from non-physical causes has more limited eligibility.

step: Decide whether to remain in KiwiSaver or opt out within the 56-day window
deadline_label: Opt-out form KS10 must be filed with IR within 56 days of the first payday
non_obvious_official_guidance: New employees are automatically enrolled in KiwiSaver from their first payday and may opt out by filing form KS10 within 56 days of the first payday.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Migrant workers on temporary visas are fully subject to auto-enrolment. If the 56-day window is missed, contributions cannot be stopped until a savings-suspension is approved by IR. All contributions made before opting out are locked until age 65 — with a limited early-withdrawal right only on permanent emigration from NZ. Migrants who intend to return home within a few years often prefer to opt out and preserve liquidity rather than lock funds offshore.
non_obvious_action_required: Make the opt-out decision before the first payday if possible. If staying enrolled, elect a contribution rate (3%, 4%, 6%, 8%, or 10%); default is 3%. Note that the employer must contribute a minimum 3% while the employee remains enrolled.

step: Track days present in NZ to determine when the 183-day tax residency threshold is crossed
deadline_label: Tax residency attaches automatically on the day the 183-day count is crossed in any rolling 12-month period
non_obvious_official_guidance: A person becomes a NZ tax resident after being present in New Zealand for more than 183 days in any 12-month period.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 12-month window is rolling, not tied to the calendar year or the NZ tax year (1 April–31 March). The day-count can cross 183 days much sooner than a first-anniversary approach would suggest. Once tax residency is established, the person is liable for NZ tax on worldwide income — triggering disclosure obligations for foreign rental income, dividends, and offshore investment fund interests (FIF regime).
non_obvious_action_required: Maintain a travel diary from arrival day. Obtain tax advice around the date you expect to cross 183 days, especially if you have significant foreign assets or income. Do not wait until the end of the tax year to assess residency status.

step: Elect transitional resident status to shelter eligible foreign income for up to 4 tax years
deadline_label: Must operate from the date tax residency commences; cannot be backdated or applied to a prior year
non_obvious_official_guidance: Eligible new tax residents may claim transitional resident status, exempting most foreign-sourced income for a period of up to 4 years from their first day of NZ tax residency.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The exemption is not automatic — it operates by omitting exempt foreign income from NZ returns. It is permanently forfeited if the individual has been a NZ tax resident at any point in the 10 years before current arrival. The 4-year window cannot be extended, paused, or applied to a later year. Missing the window means full worldwide tax liability from day one of residency with no retrospective relief.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a NZ tax accountant before crossing the 183-day threshold. Confirm 10-year non-residency history with documentary evidence. Do not inadvertently include exempt foreign income in early PAYE or IR returns; correcting a misfiled return is complex and does not restart the clock.
source: Inland Revenue – Tax for new residents

step: Employer runs payday filing and begins PAYE, KiwiSaver, and ACC earner levy deductions
field_label: PAYE; KiwiSaver employer contribution; ACC earner levy
deadline_label: Filed within 2 working days of each payday

step: Maintain AEWV work conditions — work only for the accredited employer in the approved role
deadline_label: Continuous obligation for the duration of the AEWV
non_obvious_official_guidance: AEWV holders must work for the employer named on their visa in the role approved under the Job Check.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Taking on a second job — even part-time or unpaid (e.g. an unpaid director role in a family company) — without a separate visa approval is a condition breach that can trigger deportation liability. Internal promotions or significant role changes that differ from the approved Job Check description may also require a fresh Job Check and new visa application. This catches many migrants who assume normal employment flexibility applies.
non_obvious_action_required: Any role change, employer change, or additional paid or unpaid work must be assessed for visa condition impact before being actioned. Do not accept secondary work of any kind without first obtaining immigration legal advice.
source: Immigration New Zealand – Accredited Employer Work Visa

step: Initiate AEWV renewal at least 90 days before visa expiry
field_label: Visa expiry date; renewal application reference
deadline_label: Apply at least 90 days before current AEWV expiry to maintain bridging status if processing is delayed
source: Immigration New Zealand – Accredited Employer Work Visa

step: File annual NZ income tax return (IR3) or confirm automatic assessment applies
field_label: Annual tax return; refund or residual income tax payable
deadline_label: 7 July following the 31 March tax year end; extended to 31 March of the following year if filing through a registered tax agent
non_obvious_official_guidance: Most salary and wage earners receive an automatic end-of-year income tax assessment from Inland Revenue; those with other income sources must file an IR3.
non_obvious_actual_reality: New migrants commonly assume that PAYE means no annual return is required. However, any non-PAYE income — including foreign income that is no longer exempt once the 4-year transitional resident window closes — must be declared via an IR3. Failing to file when required results in late-filing penalties and use-of-money interest that accrue automatically.
non_obvious_action_required: After each 31 March tax year end, confirm with IR whether an automatic assessment has been issued. If you have any income beyond salary — rental, freelance, or overseas — file an IR3. Engage a tax agent if the transitional resident window has closed or is approaching expiry.
source: Inland Revenue – Individual income tax return IR3

step: Check whether home country has a social security agreement with NZ to avoid double contributions
field_label: Certificate of coverage; social security agreement
deadline_label: Confirm before or at the start of NZ employment
non_obvious_official_guidance: New Zealand has bilateral social security agreements with several countries that may affect liability to pay social security contributions in both countries simultaneously.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Unlike EU-to-EU moves, most non-Australian migrants to NZ find no comprehensive totalization agreement exists with their home country. Migrants from countries without an agreement may be obligated to continue contributing to their home country social security system while also paying NZ ACC levies and KiwiSaver contributions — effectively double-funding retirement and accident insurance. Countries with some form of NZ agreement include Australia (pension purposes), Canada, Ireland, and a small number of others.
non_obvious_action_required: Verify whether your home country has an active social security agreement with NZ. If on a short-term assignment under 2 years, seek a certificate of coverage from your home country authority if eligible. If no agreement exists, budget for concurrent contribution costs and assess whether KiwiSaver opt-out is appropriate to limit double exposure.
source: Work and Income NZ – International social security agreements
